# Insulated cable and long-line signalling (`submarine_cable`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/electricity.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Electricity & electronics (`electricity`)
- Deps: needs electric_telegraph, wire_drawing; helped by ohms_law_circuits, rubber_vulcanisation, differential_equations
- Core idea: A wire under water or underground needs a continuous waterproof insulating coat. Gutta-percha, the latex of a Malayan tree, softens in hot water, can be pressed seamlessly round a stranded copper core and stays tight in cold sea water; outside goes tarred hemp and an armour of iron wires. A long cable behaves like a long Leyden jar: it has to be charged before the signal appears at the far end, so signals smear out and the usable speed falls with the square of the length. The cure is a thick, pure copper core, thick insulation, low voltage and a very sensitive receiver (mirror galvanometer), never more voltage.
- Pitfalls:
  - Forcing signals through with high voltage: 2,000 volts from induction coils destroyed the insulation of the already defective 1858 Atlantic cable within weeks
  - Leaving gutta-percha exposed to sunlight and air during storage, or allowing joints or damaged insulation to admit seawater
  - Not testing the copper and every length of insulation before laying; one pinhole ruins the whole cable
  - Assuming a submarine cable can be worked as fast as a land line of the same length
- History: europe: 1843 – gutta-percha brought to London from Singapore (Montgomerie), where Malay craftsmen already used it; 1847 Siemens' press for seamless coating; 1851 lasting Dover–Calais cable; 1854–1855 William Thomson's theory of signal retardation; global: 1858 – first Atlantic cable works for a few weeks; 1866 lasting Atlantic cable laid by the Great Eastern; 1870 Britain–India, 1871 extended to China and Australia
- Read:
  - John Steele Gordon, A Thread Across the Ocean (2002)
  - Bern Dibner, The Atlantic Cable (1959)
